Describe
də-skrīb'
v. (to write down, to survey and record in writing; in Joshua, to map the land)
Latin describere, to write down or copy out, from de-, down, and scribere, to write. In Joshua 18 the Hebrew kathab means simply to write, and the writing is a survey.

Biblical Definition

The word belongs almost entirely to one scene, and it is a scene about faith. Seven tribes had not yet taken their inheritance, and Joshua rebukes their slackness, then sets them a task: “Give out from among you three men for each tribe: and I will send them, and they shall rise, and go through the land, and describe it according to the inheritance of them” (Jos 18:4). The survey is to be written in parts: “Ye shall therefore describe the land into seven parts, and bring the description hither to me, that I may cast lots for you here before the LORD our God” (Jos 18:6). And they went: “Joshua charged them that went to describe the land, saying, Go and walk through the land, and describe it, and come again to me” (Jos 18:8). Notice what order the two acts take. Men walk the ground and write it down honestly; then the lot is cast before the LORD, who disposes it. Human diligence does not compete with divine appointment here, it serves it — nobody drew a boundary to favour his tribe, because the lot was thrown after the writing. Proverbs states the principle: the lot is cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to describe as to delineate or mark the form or figure of; and to represent a thing in words, by naming its properties, so that another may form a just notion of it.

expand to see more

DESCRIBE, v.t. [L. describo; de and scribo, to write.] To delineate or mark the form or figure; as, to describe a circle.

2. To make or exhibit a figure by motion.

3. To show or represent to others in words; to communicate the resemblance of a thing, by naming its nature, form or properties.

Go and walk through the land, and describe it. Josh. xviii.

Key Scripture

Jos 18:4 — "Give out from among you three men for each tribe: and I will send them, and they shall rise, and go through the land, and describe it according to the inheritance of them; and they shall come again to me."

Jos 18:6 — "Ye shall therefore describe the land into seven parts, and bring the description hither to me, that I may cast lots for you here before the LORD our God."

Jos 18:8 — "And the men arose, and went away: and Joshua charged them that went to describe the land, saying, Go and walk through the land, and describe it, and come again to me, that I may here cast lots for you before the LORD in Shiloh."

Pro 16:9 — "A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps."

Modern Corruption

Joshua 18 is read as bare administration, when it is one of Scripture's plainest pictures of diligent human labour and sovereign divine appointment working in one act.

expand to see more

Two opposite mistakes are made with a passage like this. The first treats the surveying as mere background — the spiritual part is the lot, and the walking and writing are what men do while waiting for God to act. The second treats the lot as decorative — the real work was the survey, and the ceremony at Shiloh simply ratified it. Joshua's procedure refuses both. He sends men to walk the whole land, on foot, and to write it down in seven parts, which is hard and unglamorous work; and then he casts lots before the LORD, so that no tribe received its portion by the skill of its own surveyors. The doctrine of providence stands exactly here. God's appointment does not make diligence unnecessary; it makes diligence safe, because a man who knows the outcome is disposed by God can do his work honestly instead of steering it.

There is a further use for the honesty of the description itself. The men were charged to describe the land as it was, not as their tribe would wish it to be, and they did this before knowing which part would fall to them. That is the only condition under which a survey can be trusted, and it is a principle with wide application — a man who must divide anything is far more equitable when he does not yet know which share is his. Scripture's own practice of description follows the same rule. The histories record the sins of the patriarchs, the failures of the kings, and the quarrels of the apostles, describing the land as it is; a book that flattered its heroes would be easier to believe about nothing. Where modern retellings smooth the record, they are not improving the description, they are drawing the boundary before the lot is cast.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kathab (H3789), to write, rendered describe in Joshua 18; with goral (H1486), the lot, and nachalah (H5159), the inheritance.

expand to see more

Hebrew kathab (H3789) — to write, to inscribe; the survey of the land written in seven parts; Joshua 18:4-8.

Hebrew goral (H1486) — a lot, a pebble cast; the means by which the described land was assigned; Joshua 18:6, Proverbs 16:33.

Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a possession received rather than earned; Joshua 18:4.

Hebrew halak (H1980) — to walk, to go; go and walk through the land, the labour behind the description; Joshua 18:8.

Greek graphe (G1124) — a writing, the Scripture; the same principle that a thing written may be examined afterward; 2 Timothy 3:16.

Usage

"“Go through the land, and describe it” — the survey before the lot."

"“Bring the description hither to me” — honest work brought to the place of appointment."

"“That I may cast lots for you here before the LORD” — diligence serving providence, not competing with it."
